title: Building MCP Servers
description: The three MCP primitives (tools, resources, prompts), defining well-designed tools, resources and prompts in depth, and the SDK patterns that handle protocol details for you.

lessons.title: Tools, Resources, and Prompts: MCP's Three Primitives
lessons.description: An MCP server can offer three distinct kinds of things — and mixing them up leads to a server that's harder for clients to use well.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Define **tools**, **resources**, and **prompts** as MCP primitives and give an example of when each is the appropriate one to expose.

sections.title: 🔧 Tools: actions the model can invoke
sections.content: A **tool** is an invokable function with defined parameters that the model decides to call, exactly matching the tool-calling concept from the LLM Engineering and Agents courses — searching a database, sending a message, running a calculation. This is **model-controlled**: the LLM decides when and whether to call a given tool, based on the same tool-design principles (clear names, unambiguous descriptions) covered in the Agents course.

sections.title: 📄 Resources: data the application can attach to context
sections.content: A **resource** is a piece of data (a file's contents, a database record, a document) that the host application can read and include in the model's context — but unlike a tool, invoking a resource isn't necessarily a decision the model makes turn-by-turn; it's often something the **application** decides to attach (a user selecting a file to discuss, an application including a relevant document by default), more similar to how RAG's retrieved documents get placed into context than to a model-initiated tool call.

sections.title: 📝 Prompts: reusable prompt templates
sections.content: A **prompt** in MCP's sense is a reusable, parameterized prompt template that a server exposes — similar in spirit to the prompt templates from the LangChain module of the LangGraph course, but defined by the server and made available for any connecting client to use, rather than defined in each application's own code. A server might expose a 'summarize this document' prompt template that any connecting host application can offer to its users.

sections.title: 🎯 Why the distinction matters
sections.content: Each primitive has a different control model: tools are **model-invoked**, resources are typically **application-attached**, and prompts are **user- or application-selected** templates. Exposing something as the wrong primitive (a large, static reference document exposed as a 'tool' the model has to remember to call, rather than a resource the application can just attach) creates unnecessary friction and unreliability, echoing the same care needed in tool design from the Agents course, just applied to a broader set of primitive types.

sections.title: 💻 The three primitives at a glance
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Exposing static reference data as a tool instead of a resource.** This forces the model to remember to call it turn-by-turn, when the application could simply attach it whenever relevant.

**Building a 'prompt' as if it were a tool.** A prompt is a template meant to be selected and filled in, not an action with side effects — conflating the two confuses both design and client-side handling.

**Assuming every server needs all three primitives.** Plenty of well-designed servers legitimately expose only tools, or only resources — forcing an artificial use of all three adds complexity with no corresponding benefit.

questions.question: What distinguishes an MCP tool from an MCP resource in terms of who decides to use it?
options: Tools and resources are identical in every respect
A tool is invoked by the model's own decision (like tool-calling), while a resource is typically attached by the application or user, not necessarily as a model-initiated decision
Resources can only be used by MCP servers, never clients
Tools cannot have parameters, but resources can
questions.explanation: Tools follow the model-controlled tool-calling pattern from earlier courses, while resources are more like data the application chooses to attach to context, similar to RAG's retrieved documents.

questions.question: What is an MCP 'prompt' primitive?
options: A record of every past conversation with the model
A reusable, parameterized prompt template exposed by the server that any connecting client can use
A synonym for an MCP tool with no real difference
A type of resource that can never be reused
questions.explanation: MCP prompts are server-defined, reusable prompt templates — similar in spirit to LangChain's prompt templates, but made available for any connecting client rather than defined per-application.

questions.question: Why does exposing a large, static reference document as a 'tool' rather than a 'resource' create unnecessary friction?
options: Tools are always faster to use than resources
It forces the model to remember to call it turn-by-turn, rather than letting the application simply attach it as context when relevant
Resources cannot contain any static content
There's no actual difference between the two approaches
questions.explanation: Since resources are meant for data the application can attach directly, using a tool instead makes the model responsible for remembering to fetch something that could have just been included in context, adding unreliability.

questions.question: In the code example, what does the resource entry represent, and who decides to attach it?
options: A model-invoked action, decided turn-by-turn by the LLM
A file's content identified by a URI, typically attached by the application rather than invoked by the model
A reusable prompt template with parameters
A JSON-RPC error object
questions.explanation: The resource example (a file:/// URI) is exactly the kind of data an application attaches to context directly, distinct from a model-invoked tool call.

questions.question: Why would building a 'prompt' primitive as though it were a tool with side effects be a design mistake?
options: Because prompts cannot have parameters at all
Because a prompt is meant to be a selectable template to fill in, not an action the model performs, and conflating the two confuses both design and client handling
Because tools are always simpler to implement than prompts
Because MCP technically forbids servers from exposing prompts
questions.explanation: Prompts and tools serve different control models — a prompt supplies reusable template text, while a tool performs an invokable action — treating one as the other undermines the clarity each primitive is meant to provide.

questions.question: Does every well-designed MCP server need to expose all three primitives (tools, resources, and prompts)?
options: Yes, every server must expose exactly one of each
No, a server can legitimately expose only tools, or only resources, without needing to force an artificial use of all three
No, servers are limited to exposing at most one primitive type total
Yes, but only if the server uses stdio transport
questions.explanation: The three primitives exist to match different control models to different needs — not every server's use case calls for all three, and forcing them in adds unnecessary complexity.

questions.question: What real-world example does the lesson give for when a resource is application-attached rather than model-invoked?
options: A model deciding on its own, turn by turn, whether to fetch a document
A user selecting a file to discuss, or an application including a relevant document by default
The model writing a completely new document from scratch
A server refusing to expose any resources at all
questions.explanation: The lesson gives exactly these two examples — a user's file selection or an application's default inclusion — as cases where a resource gets attached by something other than the model's own turn-by-turn decision.

questions.question: How does an MCP prompt template's design goal compare to a LangChain prompt template's design goal?
options: They share no meaningful similarity at all
Both aim for a reusable, parameterized template — MCP's version is just defined by the server and made available to any connecting client rather than defined in one application's own code
LangChain prompt templates cannot accept parameters, unlike MCP prompts
MCP prompts must always be written in a different language than LangChain templates
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly draws this parallel: both are reusable, parameterized templates — the difference is where the definition lives and how portable it is across applications.

lessons.title: Defining Tools on an MCP Server
lessons.description: The same tool-design discipline from the Agents course applies directly here — an MCP server's tool definitions are exactly what the model will see.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write a well-designed MCP tool definition, applying the tool-design principles from the Agents course to the MCP context specifically.

sections.title: 📋 What a tool definition needs
sections.content:
- A clear, distinctive **name and description** — following exactly the tool-naming guidance from the Agents course's tool-use module, since an MCP client will surface this name and description to the model in precisely the same way a locally-defined tool would be.
- A **parameter schema** specifying each argument's name, type, and description, including using enums for fixed-choice parameters, exactly as covered in that same lesson.

sections.title: ⚙️ The handler: what actually runs
sections.content: Behind the tool definition sits the actual **implementation** — the code that runs when the tool is invoked, which could call an external API, query a database, or do local computation, and returns a result (or an error) back through the MCP protocol to the client, which passes it back to the model as an observation exactly as covered in the Agents course's tool-calling-mechanics lesson.

sections.title: 🎯 Applying tool-scoping principles here specifically
sections.content: The Agents course's guidance to prefer several **narrow, well-named tools** over one broad multi-purpose tool applies directly to MCP server design — an MCP server exposing a `manage_records` tool with a `mode` parameter is harder for a model to use correctly than the same server exposing `create_record`, `update_record`, and `delete_record` as three distinct, clearly-scoped tools.

sections.title: ⚠️ A tool-definition mistake specific to MCP servers
sections.content: Because an MCP server might be used by many different host applications and models the server author never anticipated, vague tool descriptions that 'made sense in context' for one specific application are especially risky — a good MCP tool description should be **self-contained and clear** without relying on assumptions about what other tools or context a connecting application happens to also provide, since the server author usually can't know that in advance.

sections.title: 💻 A narrow tool definition vs. a broad one
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Writing a tool description that only makes sense for one anticipated application.** Since a server may be used by host applications the author never imagined, descriptions need to be self-contained rather than relying on assumed surrounding context.

**Reaching for a broad `mode`-parameter tool for convenience.** It reduces the number of tool definitions to write, but makes correct tool selection harder for the model — the opposite of what the Agents course's tool-scoping guidance recommends.

**Treating the handler's correctness as separate from the tool definition's clarity.** A perfectly correct implementation behind a vague, ambiguous description still produces unreliable tool selection, since the model only ever sees the definition, not the code.

questions.question: What tool-design principle from the Agents course applies directly to defining an MCP server's tools?
options: Tool names and descriptions don't matter for MCP servers since a client handles everything automatically
Clear, distinctive names and descriptions, since the client surfaces these to the model exactly as it would for a locally-defined tool
MCP tools should always use a single 'mode' parameter to reduce tool count
Parameter schemas are unnecessary for MCP tools
questions.explanation: MCP doesn't change how the model sees tool names and descriptions — the same clarity and specificity guidance from the Agents course's tool-design lesson applies directly.

questions.question: Why is preferring several narrow tools over one broad multi-purpose tool with a mode parameter still good advice for MCP servers?
options: It isn't good advice — MCP servers should always use one big tool for efficiency
A narrow, clearly-scoped tool is easier for a model to select correctly, exactly as covered in the Agents course's tool-use module
MCP technically prohibits multi-purpose tools
Narrow tools require less code to implement
questions.explanation: This is a direct application of the Agents course's tool-scoping guidance to the MCP context — narrow, well-named tools remain easier to select correctly than one broad tool gated by a mode parameter.

questions.question: Why is a vague tool description especially risky specifically for an MCP server (versus a tool defined directly in one application)?
options: Vague descriptions are never a problem for any kind of tool
An MCP server might be used by many different host applications the author never anticipated, so descriptions relying on assumed context from one specific application are unreliable elsewhere
MCP servers cannot have descriptions at all
This risk only applies to resources, never to tools
questions.explanation: Since an MCP server's tools may be consumed by unknown future applications, descriptions need to be self-contained and clear without relying on assumptions specific to any one connecting application.

questions.question: In the code example, what is the specific downside of the manage_records tool compared to the three narrow tools?
options: It cannot be registered with the SDK's decorator at all
It bundles create/update/delete behind a mode parameter, making it harder for a model to select and use correctly than three distinct, clearly-scoped tools
It has no implementation code behind it
It requires a different transport than the narrow tools
questions.explanation: The example shows exactly the Agents course's scoping guidance: one broad tool gated by a mode string versus three self-explanatory tools that are each easier to select correctly.

questions.question: What does the 'handler' behind a tool definition actually do?
options: It only stores the tool's name and description with no executable logic
It's the actual implementation code that runs when the tool is invoked, returning a result or error back through the MCP protocol
It replaces the need for a parameter schema
It is only relevant for resources, not tools
questions.explanation: The handler is where the real work happens — calling an API, querying a database, or computing something — with its result or error passed back through MCP to the client and then to the model.

questions.question: Why can a perfectly correct tool handler still lead to unreliable tool selection?
options: Because handlers are never actually executed by MCP servers
Because the model only ever sees the tool's definition (name, description, parameters) — a vague or ambiguous definition produces poor selection regardless of how correct the underlying code is
Because correct handlers always guarantee correct tool selection
Because MCP hides all handler code from the model, making descriptions irrelevant
questions.explanation: Tool selection is driven entirely by what the model can see — the definition — so implementation correctness behind an unclear description doesn't fix a tool-selection problem.

questions.question: Why might a server author be tempted to write a single broad tool with a mode parameter, and why is this still a mistake?
options: It's tempting because it's technically required by MCP, and it's not actually a mistake
It's tempting because it reduces the number of definitions to write, but it makes correct tool selection harder for the model, contradicting the Agents course's scoping guidance
It's tempting because narrow tools cannot be registered via decorators
It's tempting because broad tools always run faster than narrow ones
questions.explanation: The convenience of writing fewer definitions doesn't offset the cost to model reliability that a broad, mode-gated tool introduces — narrow tools remain the better design choice.

questions.question: What should a tool description avoid relying on, specifically because MCP servers may serve many different host applications?
options: Avoid relying on having a parameter schema at all
Avoid relying on assumptions about what other tools or context a specific connecting application happens to also provide
Avoid ever mentioning what the tool actually does
Avoid using enums for fixed-choice parameters
questions.explanation: Since the server author can't know every future host application's context, descriptions need to stand on their own rather than assuming context that only made sense for one anticipated use case.

lessons.title: Resources and Prompts in Depth
lessons.description: Two primitives that look simple on the surface but have their own design considerations worth getting right.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Design a resource URI scheme and a parameterized prompt template for an MCP server, and explain the design considerations behind each.

sections.title: 🔗 Resource identification
sections.content: Resources are typically identified by a **URI-like scheme** (something like `file:///path/to/doc` or a custom scheme specific to the server's domain), which lets a client refer to a specific resource unambiguously and lets a server organize its available resources in a structured, discoverable way — similar in spirit to how a well-organized API uses clear, structured endpoint paths rather than opaque identifiers.

sections.title: 📋 Listing versus reading resources
sections.content: MCP typically separates **'what resources are available'** (a listing operation, potentially with resource metadata like a name and description, similar to how tool listings work) from **'give me this specific resource's actual content'** (a read operation) — this separation matters for the same reason curating a relevant tool subset mattered in the Agents course's tool-selection-at-scale lesson: an application might want to show available resources to a user without eagerly fetching the full content of every single one.

sections.title: 📝 Designing a good prompt template
sections.content: An MCP prompt template accepts **parameters** (similar to a tool's parameters) that get filled in to produce the actual prompt text — designing these well means the same things that made a good prompt template in the LangChain course's prompt-template lesson: clear placeholder names, sensible handling of optional parameters, and instructions that produce consistent results regardless of which host application ends up using the template.

sections.title: 🔀 Dynamic resources and prompts
sections.content: Beyond a fixed, static list, both resources and prompts can be **dynamic** — a server might expose resources that reflect live data (today's log file, the current state of a record) or a prompt template whose exact content depends on some server-side state, in which case the same freshness considerations that motivated RAG over static fine-tuned facts apply here too: a resource is valuable specifically because it reflects current state at the time it's read, not a stale snapshot baked in earlier.

sections.title: 💻 Listing vs. reading, and a prompt template
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Eagerly fetching every resource's full content during listing.** This defeats the purpose of separating listing from reading and can waste significant work when a user or application only needs to see what's available.

**Baking a stale snapshot into a resource instead of reading live state.** A resource's value often comes specifically from reflecting current data at read time — a stale snapshot undermines that value the same way a stale fine-tuned fact undermines RAG's freshness argument.

**Writing prompt templates with unclear placeholder names or inconsistent optional-parameter handling.** This produces inconsistent results across different host applications using the same template, exactly the kind of design failure the LangChain prompt-template lesson warns against.

questions.question: How are MCP resources typically identified?
options: By a randomly generated number with no structure
By a URI-like scheme that lets a client refer to a specific resource unambiguously and lets a server organize resources in a structured way
Resources cannot be individually identified in MCP
By the exact same identifier used for every resource on a server
questions.explanation: A URI-like identification scheme provides structured, unambiguous references to resources, similar to how well-organized API endpoints use clear paths.

questions.question: Why does MCP typically separate listing resources from reading a specific resource's full content?
options: This separation serves no practical purpose
It lets an application show available resources to a user without eagerly fetching the full content of every one, similar to curating a relevant tool subset at scale
Listing and reading are actually the same operation with different names
Only one resource can ever exist on a server at a time
questions.explanation: Separating discovery (listing) from content retrieval (reading) avoids unnecessary work, echoing the same efficiency motivation behind curating relevant tool subsets in the Agents course.

questions.question: Why does a resource's ability to reflect live, current data matter, per this lesson?
options: Resources should always contain static, unchanging content
A resource's value often comes specifically from reflecting current state when read, similar to why RAG's retrieval is preferred over stale, fine-tuned-in facts
Live data is technically impossible to expose via MCP resources
This consideration only applies to MCP tools, never resources
questions.explanation: Just as RAG's retrieval-at-query-time beats stale facts baked into weights, a resource's usefulness often comes from reflecting genuinely current state rather than a fixed snapshot.

questions.question: In the code example, what does list_resources() return, and why doesn't it return full file contents?
options: It returns full file contents for every resource immediately
It returns only lightweight metadata (uri and name), keeping the listing operation cheap and separate from the more expensive read_resource() call
It returns nothing at all, since listing is not a supported operation
It returns the server's entire source code
questions.explanation: The example deliberately shows list_resources() returning only metadata, reserving actual content retrieval for the separate read_resource() call — exactly the listing/reading separation the lesson describes.

questions.question: What do the parameters in the summarize_document prompt template example (doc_id, length) illustrate?
options: That prompt templates cannot accept any parameters
That a prompt template accepts parameters, similar to a tool's parameters, which get filled in to produce the actual prompt text
That every prompt template must have exactly one required parameter and no optional ones
That prompt templates are identical to tools in every way
questions.explanation: The example shows parameters (doc_id required, length optional with a default) being filled into a template string, matching the lesson's description of how prompt templates work.

questions.question: Why is eagerly fetching every resource's full content during a listing operation a mistake?
options: Because listing operations are not allowed to return any data
Because it defeats the purpose of separating listing from reading and can waste significant work when only a subset of resources is actually needed
Because resources cannot have content at all
Because it would violate the JSON-RPC specification
questions.explanation: The whole point of the listing/reading split is to avoid unnecessary content-fetching work — eagerly loading everything during listing undoes that benefit.

questions.question: Why does baking a stale snapshot into a resource undermine its value, according to this lesson's freshness argument?
options: Because MCP resources are technically incapable of being stale
Because a resource is often valuable specifically because it reflects current state at read time, the same reasoning that favors RAG's retrieval over stale fine-tuned facts
Because stale resources are always faster to read than fresh ones
Because freshness is only a concern for MCP tools, not resources
questions.explanation: The lesson draws a direct parallel to RAG's freshness argument — a resource's usefulness often depends on reflecting genuinely current data rather than a fixed, outdated snapshot.

questions.question: What design failure does the lesson warn about regarding unclear placeholder names or inconsistent optional-parameter handling in prompt templates?
options: It has no real consequence since prompts are never reused
It produces inconsistent results across different host applications using the same template, echoing the same concern from the LangChain prompt-template lesson
It causes the MCP server to crash immediately on startup
It only affects resources, not prompt templates
questions.explanation: Since a prompt template may be used by many different host applications, unclear design leads to inconsistent results depending on who's using it — precisely the risk the LangChain prompt-template lesson also warns about.

lessons.title: MCP Server SDK Patterns
lessons.description: Building an MCP server from scratch by hand-implementing JSON-RPC would be needless work — SDKs handle the protocol so you focus on the actual logic.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Describe what an MCP server SDK typically handles for you and what a developer still needs to implement themselves.

sections.title: 🛠️ What the SDK handles
sections.content: The JSON-RPC message parsing and formatting covered earlier in this module, the specific MCP methods and their expected request/response shapes, and transport-level details (covered in the next module) — an SDK typically provides a **decorator- or annotation-based** way to register a plain function as a tool, resource, or prompt, handling the translation between 'a plain function in your code' and 'a properly-formatted MCP response' automatically.

sections.title: ✍️ What you still write
sections.content: The actual **logic**: what a tool does when called, what data a resource returns when read, what text a prompt template produces given its parameters. You also still write the tool/resource/prompt **metadata** (names, descriptions, parameter schemas) — the SDK doesn't know what makes a good tool description any more than a chat model API knows what makes a good prompt; the design principles from earlier in this module remain entirely the developer's responsibility.

sections.title: 🎯 A typical development pattern
sections.content:
1. Define a plain function implementing the actual logic.
2. Register it with the SDK, typically via a decorator, specifying its name, description, and parameter types — the SDK infers or validates the JSON-RPC-level details from this registration.
3. Test the function **directly** (since it's still just a plain function) before worrying about anything MCP-protocol-specific, isolating logic bugs from protocol or connection issues, much like testing a routing function in isolation from the rest of a LangGraph graph.

sections.title: ⚠️ A common SDK-era mistake
sections.content: Treating the SDK's ease of registering a function as a tool as a **substitute** for actually thinking through the tool-design principles from the Agents course — a function that was never designed with a clear name, description, or well-typed parameters doesn't become well-designed just because a decorator made it technically callable via MCP. The SDK removes protocol friction; it doesn't remove the design work.

sections.title: 💻 Decorator registration, and testing in isolation
Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Believing a decorator makes a poorly-designed tool well-designed.** Registration handles protocol plumbing only — the name, description, and parameter design still need the same care as any other tool.

**Skipping direct testing of the underlying function.** Debugging through the full MCP protocol stack when a plain function-level test would isolate the bug much faster is wasted effort.

**Assuming the SDK validates description quality.** An SDK validates structural correctness (types, required fields) — it has no way to know whether a description is actually clear or ambiguous to a model.

questions.question: What does an MCP server SDK typically handle automatically?
options: The actual business logic of every tool
JSON-RPC message parsing/formatting and the specific MCP method shapes, translating plain functions into properly-formatted MCP responses
Deciding what makes a good tool description
Writing the parameter schemas for you with no input needed
questions.explanation: SDKs abstract away the protocol-level plumbing (JSON-RPC formatting, MCP method shapes) so developers can register plain functions rather than hand-implementing the wire protocol.

questions.question: What remains the developer's responsibility even when using an MCP server SDK?
options: Nothing — the SDK handles everything automatically
The actual tool/resource/prompt logic, and the design of names, descriptions, and parameter schemas
The underlying JSON-RPC message format
The transport-level connection details
questions.explanation: The SDK removes protocol friction, but the real logic and the tool-design quality (following the Agents course's principles) still depend entirely on the developer's own choices.

questions.question: Why is testing a tool's underlying plain function directly (before worrying about the MCP protocol) a good development pattern?
options: It's not useful — only full end-to-end MCP testing matters
It isolates logic bugs from protocol or connection issues, similar to testing a routing function in isolation in LangGraph
Plain functions cannot be tested outside of MCP
This pattern is only relevant for resources, not tools
questions.explanation: Since the underlying implementation is still just a plain function, testing it directly narrows down whether a bug is in the actual logic or in the protocol/connection layer, mirroring the isolated-testing approach from the LangGraph debugging lesson.

questions.question: In the code example, why is _lookup_order_status defined as a separate plain function rather than only existing inside the decorated lookup_order_status?
options: Because decorated functions cannot contain any logic at all
So the actual logic can be tested directly, in isolation from the MCP protocol layer, exactly as the development pattern recommends
Because the SDK requires two separate function definitions for every tool
Because JSON-RPC forbids calling functions from within decorated functions
questions.explanation: Separating the plain logic function from the decorated registration lets test_lookup_order_status() exercise the real logic directly without any MCP protocol machinery involved.

questions.question: What does the @server.tool() decorator in the example handle on the developer's behalf?
options: It writes the actual order-lookup business logic automatically
It handles the registration and translation between the plain function and a properly-formatted MCP tool response, using the given name and description
It guarantees the description is clear and unambiguous to any model
It replaces the need for a database entirely
questions.explanation: The decorator's job is protocol registration and formatting — it does not, and cannot, judge whether the supplied name and description are actually well-designed.

questions.question: Why is 'a decorator made my function technically callable via MCP' not the same as 'my tool is well-designed'?
options: Because decorators actually prevent tools from being callable at all
Because callability is a protocol-level concern the SDK handles, while tool-design quality (clear names, descriptions, parameters) is a separate concern the SDK cannot judge
Because well-designed tools cannot use decorators
Because MCP tools are never technically callable regardless of registration
questions.explanation: The SDK guarantees a function is reachable via MCP once registered; it says nothing about whether the model will actually be able to select and use that tool reliably, which depends entirely on design quality.

questions.question: Why might skipping direct testing of the underlying function and only testing through the full MCP stack waste effort?
options: Because MCP-level testing is always faster than direct function testing
Because debugging through the full protocol stack to find a bug that a simple direct function-level test would isolate immediately is unnecessarily slow
Because direct function testing is technically impossible once a decorator is applied
Because the SDK forbids testing functions outside of the MCP protocol
questions.explanation: Testing the plain function directly narrows down whether a failure is a logic bug or a protocol/connection issue much faster than working through the entire MCP stack for every test.

questions.question: Can an SDK validate whether a tool's description is clear and unambiguous to a model?
options: Yes, SDKs automatically rewrite unclear descriptions
No, an SDK can validate structural correctness like types and required fields, but has no way to judge whether a description is actually clear to a model
Yes, but only for tools, never for resources or prompts
No, SDKs cannot process descriptions in any way
questions.explanation: Structural validation (types, required parameters) is within an SDK's reach, but genuine description quality is a design judgment call that remains the developer's responsibility.
